case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, based on the complaint’s alleged facts, a generic drug manufacturer can be held liable for inducing infringement of a brand manufacturer’s method-of-use patents when the generic uses a “skinny label” but its labeling and marketing conduct allegedly encourages the patented use.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) (induced infringement), in the Hatch-Waxman/ANDA context (including the “carve-out/skinny label” mechanism reflected in 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) and the patent-listing framework of 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(1) & (c)(2)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Hikma) argue that the Federal Circuit incorrectly allowed an induced-infringement claim to proceed on an expansive theory that threatens the Hatch-Waxman skinny-label pathway for launching lower-cost generics. They contend that, absent an affirmative act specifically encouraging physicians to practice the patented method (and not merely selling an AB-rated generic with an FDA-approved carve-out label), respondents have not plausibly alleged the intent and encouragement required by § 271(b). Petitioners and supporting amici (including the United States, AAM, Waxman, and scholars) emphasize that permitting inducement liability based on routine, FDA-regulated labeling/communications and foreseeable off-label or cross-label use would chill carve-outs, delay generic entry, and raise drug costs, contrary to Hatch-Waxman’s design.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Amarin) argue that the Federal Circuit correctly held that—given the particular ‘constellation of facts’ pleaded—Hikma plausibly engaged in active inducement under § 271(b). Amarin’s position is that even with a skinny label, a generic can still induce infringement if its communications (including labeling-related materials, product positioning, or marketing conduct) effectively instruct or encourage the patented method-of-use, and that the complaint plausibly alleges such affirmative encouragement and the requisite intent. Respondents characterize the decision as fact-bound and consistent with existing inducement doctrine, preserving method-of-use patent protection for new therapeutic uses while still allowing lawful carve-outs where the generic does not encourage the patented use.
key_precedents: Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. (2011)
DSU Medical Corp. v. JMS Co. (Fed. Cir. 2006) (en banc in relevant part)
MGM Studios Inc. v. Grokster, Ltd. (2005)
Warner-Lambert Co. v. Apotex Corp. (Fed. Cir. 2003)
AstraZeneca LP v. Apotex, Inc. (Fed. Cir. 2011)
Takeda Pharmaceuticals U.S.A., Inc. v. West-Ward Pharmaceutical Corp. (Fed. Cir. 2015)
GlaxoSmithKline LLC v. Teva Pharmaceuticals USA, Inc. (Fed. Cir. 2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress that a skinny label is not categorical immunity and that “labeling-adjacent” communications could, in some settings, amount to the affirmative encouragement Grokster contemplates; our holding should make that explicit to avoid any perceived safe harbor. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett underscore (invoking Global-Tech and Caraco), the complaint must still plausibly allege targeted, use-specific promotion with specific intent, not an inference drawn primarily from AB-rating, lawful launch under § 355(j), and FDA-governed communications equally consistent with noninfringing marketing. Justice Jackson’s “constellation of facts” approach has force at the Rule 12 stage, yet without concrete allegations of non-routine steering or instruction toward the patented method, it risks collapsing § 271(b)’s “actively induces” into foreseeability—destabilizing the Hatch-Waxman balance Congress designed. A narrow opinion requiring particularized allegations of affirmative, culpable encouragement preserves both inducement doctrine and the statutory carve-out pathway, while leaving room for liability where a generic actually promotes the patented use.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point—that a skinny label is not categorical immunity and that a “constellation” of conduct might sometimes show inducement—even at Rule 12—does not overcome the statutory text: § 271(b)’s “actively induces” requires plausible allegations of purposeful, affirmative encouragement directed to the patented method, not conduct equally consistent with Congress’s § 355(j) carve-out pathway. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, if AB-rating, ordinary distribution, and FDA-regulated labeling-adjacent communications suffice without more use-specific promotion or instruction, we effectively collapse specific intent into foreseeability and read “actively” out of the statute. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Caraco reinforces that Congress anticipated section viii carve-outs would permit generic entry notwithstanding predictable substitution dynamics; it would be anomalous to treat routine compliance with that mechanism as the very “affirmative act” that supplies inducement. On this pleading, absent particularized allegations of targeted promotion toward the patented use, I would not dilute Global-Tech/Grokster’s specific-intent requirement into a negligence-like standard.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right to resist any notion of categorical immunity from a skinny label, and I agree that “labeling-adjacent” conduct could, in some circumstances, satisfy § 271(b). But under the text—“actively induces”—and our specific-intent cases (Global-Tech and Grokster), the complaint must plausibly allege purposeful, culpable encouragement of the patented method, not merely facts like AB-rating, lawful launch, and FDA-regulated communications that are equally consistent with marketing only carved-out indications. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Caraco reflects Congress’s design to allow section viii carve-outs to facilitate generic entry; turning routine participation in that system and foreseeable downstream prescribing into inducement would, as a practical matter, erode the carve-out mechanism and collapse intent into foreseeability. Because the respondent’s “constellation” theory risks imposing negligence-like liability without well-pleaded, non-routine, use-specific promotional acts, I would reverse at the pleading stage.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that § 271(b) cannot be reduced to mere foreseeability plus lawful, FDA-regulated conduct, and that Congress expected section viii carve-outs to enable generic entry without automatic inducement exposure. But I do not read Global-Tech or Grokster to require, at the Rule 12 stage, the kind of granular “targeted promotion” proof they propose; plausibility can rest on a pleaded set of affirmative, “labeling-adjacent” communications and marketing acts that—taken together—reasonably permit the inference of purposeful encouragement of the patented method. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Caraco appropriately underscores the carve-out mechanism, yet Caraco does not create an inducement safe harbor when a complaint alleges the generic leveraged real-world drug information channels in ways that plausibly steer prescribers toward the patented use despite the carve-out. On my pragmatic view, given the stakes for access to justice and the risk that a heightened pleading screen functionally immunizes sophisticated inducement through indirect messaging, I would allow this plausibly pleaded claim to proceed to discovery without converting § 355(j) compliance into categorical protection.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson are right to resist any categorical “skinny label” immunity, and I agree (as the Chief Justice emphasizes) that labeling-adjacent communications could, in some settings, satisfy Grokster’s affirmative-encouragement requirement. But on these pleadings, the alleged conduct—FDA-regulated labeling consistent with a § 355(j) carve-out, AB-rating, and foreseeable substitution—remains at least as consistent with lawful marketing of noninfringing uses as with a targeted effort to promote the patented method, making the Global-Tech specific-intent inference too thin. Caraco, as Justice Barrett notes, confirms Congress designed the section viii pathway to allow generic entry without forcing generics to internalize predictable downstream prescribing; reading § 271(b) to treat those predictable market dynamics as “active inducement” would erode that structure and effectively collapse intent into foreseeability. The workable middle ground is to leave room for inducement claims when there are well-pleaded facts of affirmative steering toward the patented indication, while holding this complaint insufficient because it lacks such use-specific promotional acts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that a skinny label is not categorical immunity and that “labeling-adjacent” communications could, in some circumstances, amount to inducement; § 271(b) can reach conduct that affirmatively steers prescribers to the patented method. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress (with Barrett’s reliance on Caraco), Congress affirmatively authorized the § 355(j) carve-out pathway, and it would distort the text of § 271(b)—“actively induces”—to treat routine AB-rating, FDA-compelled labeling, and predictable substitution effects as the affirmative act or specific intent Global-Tech and Grokster require. Justice Jackson’s “constellation of facts” framing is appealing at Rule 12, yet without concrete, non-routine allegations of use-specific advocacy or instruction, the pleaded facts remain equally consistent with lawful marketing of the carved-out indications, which is insufficient under a textual, intent-centered reading of inducement. Enforcing that pleading threshold does not create a safe harbor; it simply preserves § 271(b)’s mens rea and the Hatch-Waxman balance Congress enacted.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is procedural: at Rule 12 a “constellation” of labeling-adjacent statements and market conduct might plausibly function as instruction under Grokster even without an explicit infringing label. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Global-Tech and Grokster still require plausible allegations of purposeful, culpable encouragement of the patented method—not an intent inference drawn mainly from AB-rating, lawful launch, and FDA-regulated communications that are equally consistent with Congress’s § 355(j) carve-out pathway. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Caraco reinforces that Congress expected generics to use section viii carve-outs to enter without incurring inducement liability merely from predictable substitution dynamics; letting routine compliance supply the “affirmative act” would erode § 271(b)’s specific-intent requirement and destabilize the Hatch-Waxman balance. I therefore remain with Petitioner: absent particularized allegations of targeted promotion or instruction directed to the patented use, the complaint does not plausibly plead active inducement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson rightly stress that a skinny label is not categorical immunity and that “labeling-adjacent” conduct can, in some circumstances, amount to Grokster’s “purposeful, culpable expression and conduct.” But applying a textualist reading of § 271(b) as construed in Global-Tech, the complaint still must plausibly allege specific intent—affirmative encouragement directed to the patented method—not allegations equally consistent with lawful participation in the § 355(j) carve-out pathway that Caraco recognized Congress expected generics to use. At the Rule 12 stage, requiring more particularized allegations of targeted promotion or instruction toward the patented use does not create a safe harbor; it simply prevents foreseeability and ordinary substitution dynamics from collapsing the “actively induces” element into negligence-like liability. Chief Justice Roberts’ proposed narrow approach best preserves Hatch-Waxman’s structure while leaving room for inducement claims when the pleadings identify concrete steering toward the infringing use beyond routine FDA-regulated labeling and sales.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point seriously that § 271(b) cannot collapse into foreseeability based on AB-rating, lawful launch, and FDA-regulated labeling, because Global-Tech and Grokster require purposeful, culpable encouragement of the patented method. But that concern cuts to the merits proof, not necessarily Rule 12 plausibility, where the question is whether the complaint alleges more than routine Hatch-Waxman compliance—i.e., a plausible “constellation” of labeling-adjacent communications or marketing that functions as instruction or steering toward the patented use. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Caraco reinforces that section viii carve-outs are integral to Hatch-Waxman’s design, yet Caraco does not create immunity from inducement when a generic allegedly goes beyond the carve-out pathway and affirmatively encourages the patented indication through real-world drug-information channels. Procedural fairness and practical consequences counsel allowing discovery when intent is plausibly alleged, rather than creating a pleading rule that, in operation, becomes a de facto safe harbor untethered from § 271(b)’s text and our inducement precedents.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires “active” inducement—purposeful encouragement with knowledge of the patent and that the encouraged acts constitute infringement—not mere foreseeability that some physicians will practice the patented method. Global-Tech and Grokster make clear that inducement turns on “purposeful, culpable expression and conduct,” such as advertising or instructing an infringing use, and caution against theories that would “compromise legitimate commerce.” In the Hatch-Waxman context, Congress specifically authorized the § 355(j) carve-out (skinny label) mechanism; allowing inducement claims to proceed on allegations that largely track FDA-regulated labeling and AB-rated sales risks undermining that pathway and invites overbroad liability inconsistent with the narrow, intent-focused nature of § 271(b). On these pleaded facts, I would require more particularized allegations of affirmative promotion of the patented use before permitting the claim to proceed.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who "actively induces infringement," which, as this Court held in Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., requires knowledge of the patent and a specific intent to bring about infringement, not mere foreseeability that others might use the product in an infringing way. In the Hatch-Waxman context, Congress expressly authorized a “carve-out/skinny label” pathway for nonpatented uses, 21 U.S.C. § 355(j), and courts should not expand § 271(b) to treat FDA-regulated, congressionally permitted labeling and AB-rated sales as presumptive “affirmative acts” of encouragement absent concrete allegations of purposeful, culpable conduct directed to the patented method (cf. Grokster). Taking the complaint’s allegations as true, inducement cannot be plausibly inferred from conduct that is equally consistent with lawful marketing of the carved-out uses; § 271(b) is not negligence or strict liability. Preserving the statutory balance Congress struck in Hatch-Waxman counsels against diluting § 271(b)’s specific-intent requirement at the pleading stage.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only for "actively induc[ing]" infringement, which this Court has tied to purposeful, culpable conduct—an affirmative act that encourages the patented use coupled with knowledge/intent. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. requires at least knowledge (including willful blindness) that the induced acts constitute infringement, and Grokster cautions against expansive inducement theories that would "compromise legitimate commerce" by treating routine distribution-related conduct as inducement. In the Hatch-Waxman setting, Congress specifically authorized carve-outs/"skinny labels" in 21 U.S.C. § 355(j), and allowing inducement claims to proceed based on FDA-regulated labeling and foreseeable cross-use would undermine that scheme and chill lawful generic entry. On the complaint’s alleged facts, absent specific, non-routine promotional conduct expressly encouraging the patented method, the inducement and specific-intent requirements of § 271(b) are not plausibly met.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: At the pleadings stage, § 271(b) allows liability where the complaint plausibly alleges “active” inducement—i.e., affirmative steps that encourage infringement—rather than mere lawful sale of a product capable of noninfringing use. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. teaches that inducement requires intent/knowledge (including willful blindness) and “affirmative steps,” and Grokster similarly frames inducement as turning on “culpable expression and conduct,” which can include marketing and communications that promote the infringing use. The Hatch-Waxman skinny-label pathway in 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) protects generics that carve out patented uses, but it does not create immunity where a generic’s labeling-related materials and marketing conduct allegedly steer prescribers toward the patented method despite the carve-out. Given that the complaint alleges a fact-specific “constellation” of conduct plausibly encouraging the patented use, dismissal would prematurely deny a remedy for a potentially unlawful scheme that could distort prescribing and harm patients who rely on accurate drug information.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires “active” inducement and a specific intent to bring about infringement, not mere foreseeability that physicians might use an AB-rated generic for a patented method despite a lawful carve-out. Global-Tech and Grokster emphasize “purposeful, culpable expression and conduct” directed to encouraging the infringing use; at the pleading stage, allegations tied to routine, FDA-regulated labeling and the Hatch-Waxman § 355(j) “skinny label” pathway should not suffice absent plausible facts showing affirmative promotion of the patented indication. Reading § 271(b) to allow inducement based on conduct Congress expressly authorized via § 355(j) carve-outs would undermine statutory coherence and workability by effectively penalizing compliance with the Hatch-Waxman scheme. On the complaint’s alleged facts as framed here, the safer middle-ground is to require a clearer showing of targeted encouragement and intent before permitting an inducement claim to proceed in the skinny-label context.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who "actively induces" infringement, requiring purposeful encouragement and the specific intent that another will practice the patented method, not merely the distribution of a lawful, FDA-approved generic with a carve-out label under 21 U.S.C. § 355(j). Under Global-Tech, inducement demands knowledge of the patent and culpable intent (including willful blindness), and Grokster underscores that inducement must rest on "purposeful, culpable expression and conduct," not "ordinary acts incident to product distribution." Taking the complaint’s allegations as true, tying inducement to routine, FDA-regulated labeling/AB-rating and foreseeable cross-use risks converting Hatch-Waxman’s skinny-label mechanism into a trap and diluting the statutory requirement of “active” encouragement. Absent plausible allegations of affirmative acts that specifically instruct or promote the patented use—as opposed to compliant labeling and general market presence—the claim should be dismissed at the pleading stage.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires active inducement with the requisite knowledge and specific intent, not merely foreseeable infringement arising from lawful product sales and FDA-regulated labeling in the Hatch-Waxman carve-out pathway. Under Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. and MGM v. Grokster, inducement turns on purposeful, culpable conduct—affirmative acts that encourage infringement—and broad theories risk “compromis[ing] legitimate commerce,” a practical concern heightened where Congress expressly authorized skinny labels in 21 U.S.C. § 355(j). Given that statutory scheme and the need for a workable, predictable rule that preserves generic entry, allegations grounded in routine labeling/marketing consistent with an FDA-approved carve-out should not, without more specific encouragement of the patented method, plausibly establish inducement. Respect for precedent and the Hatch-Waxman balance counsels limiting § 271(b) to clear, affirmative promotional direction to infringe, rather than allowing liability that would effectively nullify skinny labels.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only for "actively induc[ing]" infringement—requiring affirmative acts that encourage the patented method and a culpable mental state (knowledge or willful blindness that the induced acts constitute infringement). See 35 U.S.C. § 271(b); Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754, 760, 764 (2011); MGM Studios Inc. v. Grokster, Ltd., 545 U.S. 913, 936–937 (2005). In the Hatch-Waxman context, Congress expressly created the § 355(j) "section viii" carve-out mechanism on the premise that omitting the patented use from the approved label permits marketing the generic for nonpatented uses, consistent with Caraco Pharm. Labs., Ltd. v. Novo Nordisk A/S, 566 U.S. 399, 405, 415 (2012). Taking the complaint’s allegations as true, routine FDA-regulated labeling/AB-rating and lawful product distribution—without specific promotional encouragement of the patented method—does not plausibly plead the "purposeful, culpable" encouragement and intent that Global-Tech and Grokster require, and an expansive inducement theory would undercut the statutory skinny-label pathway Congress designed.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: At the pleading stage, the question is not whether inducement is ultimately proven, but whether the complaint plausibly alleges “active” encouragement and the requisite intent under 35 U.S.C. § 271(b), consistent with Global-Tech’s requirement of knowledge and purposeful facilitation rather than mere foreseeability. Accepting the alleged “constellation of facts” as true, a skinny label under 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) does not categorically immunize a generic from liability if its labeling-adjacent communications or marketing conduct plausibly function as instructions or promotion of the patented method, which Grokster recognizes as the kind of “purposeful, culpable expression and conduct” that can constitute inducement. Preserving Hatch-Waxman’s carve-out pathway is important, but procedural fairness and practical consequences cut both ways: method-of-use patents listed under 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(1) & (c)(2) are also part of Congress’s balance, and a plausibly pleaded claim of deliberate encouragement should be allowed to proceed to discovery. On these allegations, dismissal would risk converting the skinny-label mechanism into a de facto safe harbor untethered from § 271(b)’s text and this Court’s intent-focused inducement doctrine.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a generic-drug manufacturer can be held liable for inducing infringement of a brand’s method-of-use patents based on its marketing and product labeling (including a “skinny label”) when the patented use is not the FDA-approved indication the generic formally seeks to carve out.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) (induced infringement), as applied in the Hatch-Waxman framework (21 U.S.C. § 355(j); and the patent-listing/carve-out regime associated with Orange Book use codes).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Hikma) argue that the Federal Circuit improperly allowed an inducement claim to proceed on allegations that amount to lawful generic competition—selling an AB-rated generic with a carve-out label—and that inducement requires plausible allegations of (1) specific intent to cause infringement and (2) affirmative acts that actually encourage the patented use. They contend that permitting inducement based on routine communications about therapeutic equivalence, standard labeling, or the foreseeable reality of physicians prescribing off-label collapses the line between lawful sale and unlawful encouragement, undermines skinny-label carve-outs Congress contemplated under Hatch-Waxman, chills generic entry, and raises drug costs. Supporting amici (including the United States, AAM, and Rep. Waxman) emphasize that expanding inducement in this setting would effectively nullify carve-outs by making generics liable whenever some prescribers use the drug in a patented way, even absent targeted promotion of that use.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Amarin and related entities) argue that, given the specific ‘constellation of facts’ pleaded, they plausibly alleged that Hikma took affirmative steps that went beyond mere sale of a carve-out generic and intentionally encouraged the patented method of use (e.g., through how the generic was labeled, described, substituted, or promoted in the marketplace). They maintain that inducement is a fact-intensive inquiry and that the complaint adequately pleads both knowledge of the patents and purposeful conduct aimed at causing infringing use, making dismissal improper at the pleading stage. In their view, recognizing liability on these allegations does not eliminate skinny labels; it simply enforces the boundary that generics may not actively steer prescribers toward patented indications while nominally carving them out.
key_precedents: Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. (2011)
MGM Studios Inc. v. Grokster, Ltd. (2005)
Warner-Lambert Co. v. Apotex Corp. (Fed. Cir. 2003)
AstraZeneca LP v. Apotex, Inc. (Fed. Cir. 2011)
Takeda Pharmaceuticals U.S.A., Inc. v. West-Ward Pharmaceutical Corp. (Fed. Cir. 2015)
GlaxoSmithKline LLC v. Teva Pharmaceuticals USA, Inc. (Fed. Cir. 2021)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondents’ best point remains that a generic can “induce” by leveraging the predictable substitution and prescribing ecosystem even with a skinny label, but under Global-Tech and Grokster that shows, at most, foreseeability—not the “purposeful, culpable” encouragement § 271(b) requires. Justice Kagan’s workability concern most crystallizes the institutional stakes: if FDA-compliant § viii carve-outs plus routine AB-rating/equivalence communications suffice, Congress’s Hatch–Waxman compromise becomes functionally unadministrable and the word “actively” does no limiting work. Justice Thomas’s textual focus reinforces a narrow, precedent-respecting path: require plausible allegations of affirmative acts specifically directed to promoting the patented method-of-use beyond what the FDA scheme compels. On that minimal ground—essentially a pleading-line holding—we can reverse without immunizing truly promotional conduct aimed at the carved-out indication.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that AB-rating/equivalence messaging plus predictable substitution makes infringing use effectively inevitable, allowing intent to be inferred from market realities. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 271(b)’s text requires that one “actively induces” infringement, and Global-Tech and Grokster confine inducement to purposeful, culpable steps aimed at the infringing use—not lawful sales and FDA-authorized § viii carve-outs whose downstream effects are merely foreseeable. Accepting inevitability/foreseeability as a substitute for targeted encouragement would read “actively” out of the statute and, in practice, nullify Congress’s Hatch-Waxman carve-out pathway in 21 U.S.C. § 355(j). Warner-Lambert (noted by several colleagues) fits that original public meaning by rejecting inducement where the defendant’s conduct is equally explained as lawful marketing and regulatory compliance absent promotion of the patented method.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that AB-rating, substitution norms, and known off-label prescribing make infringement effectively inevitable—still proves too much under § 271(b) as construed in Global-Tech and Grokster: foreseeability (even inevitability) is not the same as purposeful, culpable encouragement. Chief Justice Roberts’s statutory-coherence concern is decisive for me: if FDA-compliant § viii carve-outs plus routine equivalence communications can alone constitute “active inducement,” Congress’s carve-out pathway becomes largely illusory, and “actively” does no real work. Justice Kagan’s administrability point reinforces that we need a clear line between lawful generic entry and targeted promotion of the patented method; the complaint here alleges the former but not the latter. No colleague has identified precedent that would allow intent to be inferred from regulated, ordinary-market conduct without some affirmative step aimed at the carved-out use, so I remain for reversal and dismissal on these pleadings.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that, in the real world, a skinny label plus AB-rating can predictably channel use toward the patented indication—but that is still not the “purposeful, culpable” encouragement Global-Tech and Grokster require, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress. Treating FDA-compliant carve-outs and routine therapeutic-equivalence communications as inducement would, as Justice Kagan explains, make Congress’s § viii pathway largely self-defeating and chill generic entry that expands access. I also agree with Justice Jackson that, at the pleading stage, fairness and administrability require concrete allegations of targeted promotion of the carved-out patented method, not an inference of intent from foreseeable substitution dynamics. On this complaint, the allegations read as lawful competition within a regulated scheme rather than affirmative acts aimed at inducing the patented use.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that AB-rating, substitution dynamics, and predictable off-label prescribing show “intent” even with a § viii carve-out—still collapses § 271(b) into foreseeability-plus-sales, which Global-Tech and Grokster do not allow; they require purposeful, culpable affirmative conduct aimed at the patented method. Chief Justice Roberts’s statutory-coherence concern is decisive for me: if FDA-compliant skinny labeling and routine equivalence communications can be recast as “active inducement,” Congress’s § viii pathway becomes practically self-defeating. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on the text “actively induces” reinforces an administrable line that distinguishes lawful market entry from targeted encouragement of the carved-out use. On these pleadings, without concrete allegations of promotion or messaging directed to the patented indication, dismissal best preserves both doctrinal clarity and the Hatch-Waxman balance while leaving room for liability where a generic actually markets the patented method.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that AB-rating/equivalence messaging plus predictable substitution can functionally channel use toward the patented method, permitting an inference of intent from market realities. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, § 271(b)’s text—“actively induces”—as understood in Global-Tech and Grokster, requires purposeful, affirmative steps aimed at promoting the infringing use; lawful sales coupled with foreseeability (even near-inevitability) are not enough, or else “actively” does no work. Justice Kagan’s workability concern reinforces the statutory-coherence problem: if Hatch-Waxman-compliant § viii carve-outs and the ordinary incidents of FDA-regulated equivalence communications can alone establish inducement, Congress’s carve-out pathway in 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) becomes largely illusory. Warner-Lambert, invoked by several colleagues, cuts against respondent rather than for it, because it illustrates that absent targeted promotion of the patented indication, lawful marketing and downstream physician behavior do not plausibly plead specific intent to induce.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that a generic can “intend” infringement by leveraging predictable substitution and off-label prescribing even with a skinny label, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, Global-Tech and Grokster require purposeful, culpable steps directed to the patented use—not mere foreseeability plus lawful sales into a regulated market. Treating FDA-compliant § viii carve-outs and routine AB-rating/equivalence communications as “active inducement” would, as Roberts emphasizes, undermine Congress’s Hatch-Waxman compromise and make the carve-out pathway largely illusory, a practical consequence we should avoid for institutional and statutory-coherence reasons. Justice Thomas’s textual point about giving meaning to “actively induces” reinforces that line: inducement must rest on concrete promotional conduct encouraging the patented method, not the ordinary incidents of lawful generic entry. Warner-Lambert fits that framework by rejecting inducement absent targeted encouragement, so I remain for reversal and an administrable rule requiring plausible allegations of promotion aimed at the carved-out use.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point—that a generic’s awareness of automatic substitution and widespread off-label prescribing makes infringement effectively intended—still collapses § 271(b)’s “actively induces” into mere foreseeability, contrary to Global-Tech and Grokster’s requirement of purposeful, affirmative conduct aimed at the infringing use. Chief Justice Roberts’s statutory-coherence argument is decisive for me as a textualist: treating FDA-compliant § viii carve-out labeling and routine AB-rating/equivalence communications as “active” inducement would make Congress’s carve-out pathway practically self-defeating. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern reinforces that we need a workable line: absent allegations of targeted promotion (or comparable affirmative encouragement) of the carved-out patented method, the complaint describes lawful market entry plus predictable third-party behavior, not inducement. Warner-Lambert, invoked by several colleagues, fits that framework by rejecting inducement based on lawful marketing and foreseeable downstream infringement without additional encouraging acts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that AB-rating and predictable substitution make infringement practically inevitable, but inevitability is not the same as the “purposeful, culpable” encouragement required by Global-Tech and Grokster. Chief Justice Roberts’s statutory-balance concern is persuasive to me as a matter of procedural fairness and practical consequences: if FDA-compliant § viii skinny labeling plus routine equivalence/AB-rating communications can plead § 271(b) inducement, Congress’s carve-out pathway becomes self-defeating and litigation-risk would chill lawful generic entry. Justice Kagan’s administrability point reinforces a workable pleading line—courts should require concrete allegations of targeted promotion of the carved-out patented use, not infer specific intent from conduct equally consistent with regulatory compliance and lawful competition. No colleague has identified precedent that undermines that intent requirement; Warner-Lambert, as several note, fits the view that lawful marketing plus foreseeable downstream infringement is not enough without affirmative encouragement aimed at the patented method.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires not only knowledge but “specific intent and action to induce infringement,” Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754 (2011), and inducement cannot rest on conduct Congress affirmatively authorized as a pathway for generic entry under Hatch-Waxman, including a section viii carve-out label, 21 U.S.C. § 355(j). Under Warner-Lambert Co. v. Apotex Corp., 316 F.3d 1348 (Fed. Cir. 2003), lawful marketing and regulatory compliance—even with foreseeable downstream infringing use—do not, without more, establish inducement; allowing routine AB-rating/equivalence communications or carve-out labeling to suffice would effectively nullify the skinny-label regime. To preserve institutional legitimacy and the statutory balance Congress struck, I would reverse and require allegations of affirmative promotional steps specifically directed to the patented method-of-use, not merely sales and FDA-mandated labeling realities. A narrow ruling clarifying the pleading boundary for inducement in the carve-out context best respects precedent and federalism-based allocation of regulatory roles.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who "actively induces infringement," which, under its ordinary meaning and this Court’s interpretation, requires purposeful, culpable conduct aimed at bringing about infringement—not merely selling a lawful product and providing labeling information that could be foreseeably used off-label. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. makes clear that inducement requires knowledge (or willful blindness) and “active steps” to encourage infringement, and Grokster similarly limits inducement to “purposeful, culpable expression and conduct,” not ordinary incidents of product distribution. In the Hatch-Waxman context, allowing inducement based on an AB-rated generic with a carve-out label and routine equivalence communications would effectively read “actively” out of § 271(b) and undermine the statutory carve-out mechanism in 21 U.S.C. § 355(j). On the pleaded facts as framed, the allegations amount to lawful generic competition rather than targeted encouragement of the patented method-of-use, so dismissal is warranted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces infringement,” which this Court has read to require affirmative steps taken with the specific intent to bring about infringement, not merely lawful conduct that foreseeably enables it. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754, 760 (2011), together with MGM Studios Inc. v. Grokster, Ltd., 545 U.S. 913, 936–937 (2005), cautions against expanding inducement theories that would “compromise legitimate” competition absent culpable, targeted encouragement. In the Hatch-Waxman context, allowing inducement to rest on routine AB-rating communications, standard labeling, and predictable off-label prescribing would effectively nullify Congress’s carve-out mechanism under 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) and collapse the line between permissible sale and unlawful inducement under § 271(b). On these pleadings, the alleged conduct sounds more in lawful generic marketing than “affirmative acts” purposefully promoting the patented method of use, so dismissal is warranted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires purposeful, affirmative encouragement of infringement, not merely lawful sale in a setting where off-label use is foreseeable; Global-Tech’s specific-intent requirement and Grokster’s focus on deliberate promotion counsel against imposing inducement liability based on routine AB-rating/therapeutic-equivalence communications and FDA-compliant labeling. In the Hatch-Waxman framework, Congress expressly contemplated carve-outs (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)) to speed generic entry while respecting method-of-use patents, and allowing inducement claims to proceed on thin allegations tied to “skinny labels” risks functionally nullifying that balance and raising drug prices, disproportionately harming vulnerable patients’ access. Consistent with Caraco’s recognition of the carve-out/use-code regime’s role in preserving generic competition, I would require a clearer pleading of targeted promotion of the patented use—beyond compliant labeling and generalized marketplace substitution dynamics—before allowing § 271(b) liability to attach. Because the allegations here appear to collapse the line between lawful generic competition and intentional encouragement of a carved-out patented use, dismissal is warranted absent more specific affirmative acts directed at the patented indication.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires “active” inducement—affirmative acts undertaken with specific intent to bring about infringement—not merely knowledge or foreseeability that some physicians may prescribe the generic for a patented use. Under the Hatch-Waxman framework, 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) and the § viii carve-out mechanism contemplate lawful generic entry with a “skinny label,” and treating AB-rating/equivalence communications and FDA-compliant carved-out labeling as inducement would, as a practical matter, nullify that statutory compromise and undermine workability. Consistent with Global-Tech and Warner-Lambert, a complaint must plausibly allege targeted, unambiguous encouragement of the patented method (beyond lawful sale and label carve-out) to show specific intent; allegations resting on routine market realities and substitution practices are insufficient at the pleading stage. Preserving statutory coherence and the administrable boundary Congress drew requires rejecting inducement liability on these thin allegations while leaving room for liability where a generic actually promotes the carved-out patented use.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 271(b) by its plain terms reaches only those who "actively induce" infringement, and this Court has held inducement demands both knowledge of the patent and specific intent—"purposeful, culpable expression and conduct"—not mere foreseeability that others might infringe. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754, 766, 768 n.8 (2011), and MGM v. Grokster, 545 U.S. 913, 937 (2005), make clear that lawful sales and routine communications cannot be converted into inducement absent affirmative steps aimed at promoting the patented use. In the Hatch-Waxman setting, Congress expressly authorized section viii carve-outs (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)) to permit generic entry for nonpatented indications; allowing inducement liability based on a skinny label and generalized equivalence marketing would effectively nullify that statutory pathway and expand § 271(b) beyond its original, active-encouragement meaning. At the pleading stage, allegations must plausibly show targeted encouragement of the patented method of use, not just knowledge plus the predictable reality of off-label prescribing.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 271(b) requires “active” inducement—affirmative steps taken with the purpose of bringing about infringement—not merely the sale of a lawful product and the foreseeable possibility of off-label use. Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. and MGM v. Grokster insist on specific intent and “purposeful, culpable expression and conduct,” which is not satisfied by routine Hatch-Waxman compliance measures such as an FDA-approved section viii carve-out (“skinny label”) and ordinary equivalence communications absent targeted encouragement of the patented method. Allowing inducement liability to proceed on such allegations risks collapsing the statutory carve-out regime Congress created in 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) and undermines the workability of skinny labels by effectively exposing generics to liability whenever some prescribers use the drug in a patented way. Given those practical consequences and the need for a clear, administrable line that preserves lawful generic entry, the complaint should be dismissed unless it plausibly alleges concrete promotional acts that specifically encourage the patented use beyond the carved-out label.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 271(b) imposes liability only on one who “actively induces infringement,” which, under its ordinary meaning, requires affirmative steps taken with the purpose of bringing about infringing acts—not merely selling a product that could foreseeably be used in an infringing way. Global-Tech holds that inducement demands knowledge of the patent and conduct evidencing “specific intent” to cause infringement; willful blindness can satisfy the knowledge element, but foreseeability and routine, carve-out-compliant labeling or AB-rating communications do not by themselves plausibly allege the required purposeful encouragement. Allowing inducement to proceed based largely on the predictable reality of off-label prescribing would effectively collapse the statutory line between direct infringement under § 271(a) and indirect liability under § 271(b), and it would undermine Hatch-Waxman’s carve-out regime in 21 U.S.C. § 355(j) that contemplates lawful generic entry with a “skinny label.” At the pleading stage, the complaint must plausibly allege targeted promotional or labeling acts that actually encourage the patented method-of-use, and absent such allegations, dismissal is warranted to maintain methodological consistency with Global-Tech and Grokster.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under 35 U.S.C. § 271(b), inducement requires both knowledge and “specific intent” plus “affirmative acts” that actually encourage infringement, not merely the lawful sale of an AB-rated generic with an FDA-authorized carve-out under Hatch-Waxman (21 U.S.C. § 355(j)). Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A. makes clear that inducement turns on purposeful conduct directed to infringement, and extending liability based on routine equivalence communications or foreseeable off-label prescribing risks collapsing the line between permissible competition and unlawful encouragement. Given Congress’s carve-out scheme and the practical consequences for generic entry and drug costs, a skinny label should not become presumptive evidence of inducement absent targeted promotion of the patented method-of-use. Procedural fairness also counsels against allowing pleading-stage inducement claims that effectively penalize compliance with the Hatch-Waxman framework rather than requiring concrete allegations of intentional encouragement of the carved-out use.
